messages.body_plain:
Sorry, it looks like the list stripped the text of my previous message, so here it is again without the images.

I am a student working on neuroimaging. I found a repeated linear search in ehg191 that makes predict.loess(se = TRUE) much slower than it needs to be. It is still present in R-devel r90840 (src/library/stats/src/loessf.f, lines 799 to 809).

For every training observation and every k-d tree vertex, the routine scans that vertex's neighbour list backwards, so with a fixed span the search work grows with n squared. This is the path ggplot2's geom_smooth(method = "loess") takes by default, since it draws a confidence band, so I suspect quite a few people wait on it without knowing why.

The proof of concept (ehg191-lookup.diff.txt, attached to my previous message: https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-devel/attachments/20261105/f1a77502/attachment.txt) builds the inverse neighbour positions once and replaces the scan with a lookup.

On an Apple M4 chip, predicting at 80 points with n = 40,000 and span = 0.5 took 24.2 s before and 0.22 s after (medians of three paired runs). L and the full prediction result were bit for bit identical in every timing configuration and in 1,000 random configurations with one to three predictors, and 24 further fits, including statistics = "exact", were identical too.

I think the slow part can be reproduced with:

set.seed(20261105)
n <- 20000L
x <- runif(n, -3, 3)
y <- sin(x) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.35)
f <- loess(y ~ x)
nd <- data.frame(x = seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = 80L))
system.time(predict(f, nd, se = TRUE))

I rebuilt the trunk loess.R, loessc.c and loessf.f, unchanged and patched, under R 4.5.2 on macOS arm64.

Would this be worth turning into a proper patch with a regression test? I would be glad of advice on how you would prefer the workspace to be allocated.

Thanks,
Don

messages.body_plain:
Hi Toby and all,

The list rejected my last message because of the images (again, sorry), so here it is again in text for everyone else. Toby, sorry for the duplicate.

I don't think the error comes from the patch. Stock R 4.5.2 and the unpatched trunk sources stop with the same message, and the same number, at N = 39810:

workspace required (2377642345) is too large probably because of setting 'se = TRUE'.

With se = TRUE, loess needs a workspace of roughly (D + 1) x nf x N doubles, and with the default span = 0.75 that passes INT_MAX at about N = 37,800. Without the patch your atime run reaches the 1 second limit long before that, so it never gets there. That's also why I used span = 0.5 for my N = 40,000 timings.

The patch itself only adds an integer array of nv x N, and nv is 9 here, so about 1.3 MB at N = 37,000.

On the scaling: unpatched predict took 0.08, 1.1, 5.2 and 24.2 s for N = 5,000, 10,000, 20,000 and 40,000 at span = 0.5. So below 10,000 it is much steeper than quadratic for me too, then close to quadratic up to 40,000. I'm not sure yet where the extra at small N comes from.

Thanks,
Don

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I hope I am writing to the correct list. I am hoping to make a feature request for R, and I found a guide that says to write to r-devel first to check if there is support for the idea.

The feature I want to suggest is an option similar to options(warnPartialMatchDollar=TRUE), but for cases where rather than being a partial match, the variable name is misspelled or simply doesn?t exist and attempting to use it produces NULL.

This behavior of $ can sometimes lead to unexpected outcomes, as demonstrated below:

dat <- data.frame(column1=1:3,column2=NA)
stopifnot(!any(is.na(dat$coluumn2)))
stopifnot(sum(dat$coluumn1) < 2)

In both cases, the data.frame returning NULL with a misspelled column name leads to the check in the stopifnot() silently succeeding with no warning that anything might be wrong.

I know there are reasons why $ returns NULL, and I?m not suggesting changing that. Just possibly adding an option, something like options(warnNonexistDollar=TRUE), that people could turn on if they would find it helpful to get a warning in cases like the example above.

Is this something that?s likely to have enough support to be worth submitting as a feature request?

Thank you,
Kristen

    > stopifnot(sum(dat$coluumn1) < 2)

    > In both cases, the data.frame returning NULL with a misspelled column name leads to the check in the stopifnot() silently succeeding with no warning that anything might be wrong.

    > I know there are reasons why $ returns NULL, and I?m not suggesting changing that. Just possibly adding an option, something like options(warnNonexistDollar=TRUE), that people could turn on if they would find it helpful to get a warning in cases like the example above.

    > Is this something that?s likely to have enough support to be worth submitting as a feature request?

    > Thank you,

Thank you, Kirsten,

for opening an interesting issue.
Personally I'm guessing that such a warning may not be very
useful as I expect it to be triggered too often.
Notably it has been a "trick" already in S, S-plus, for a really
fast test if a list component to be present,
to have something like

   if(!is.null(cm <- mylist$comp)) {
     .....
     <work with> `cm`
     .....
   } else { 
     ## work without `cm`, in some cases just
     stop("component `comp` does not exist -- cannot do xyz")
   }

*HOWEVER*, I think the problem you really may want to solve
is the use inside stopifnot():

The "problem" is that    all( logical(0) )  is TRUE
and _should_ be {all elements of the empty set are TRUE .. etc},
i.e., the "problem" is the specification of the  stopifnot()
function --- I added to R a *long* time ago, that it can and
often should be used "vectorized", i.e.,

  stopifnot( x == y )

should be 'fine' (in simple vector/matrix/array cases)  when x
and y have the same lengths and all their corresponding elements
x[i], y[i]  are equal.

Hence stopifnot() uses internally code which may be simplified to
all(x == y).

Really experienced R users (say 0.025% of all ;-) of course are
aware of that .. but it may still be considered "dangerous"
behaviour, a really bad case being

    stopifnot(dim(x) == dim(y))

to check if two matrices (or arrays) are compatible.  If one of
x or y is accidentally a vector instead of a matrix, the above
never signals the desired error.

Hence, for many years, I have mused about, but never posted (nor
even discussed IIRC within the R core team ..)
an official proposal to eventually *change* stopifnot's default
behavior, and to eventually *warn* when its call to all(.) would be applied to
an object of length 0.
Again this makes too many uses unuseful, so I have had (starting from
on April 13, 2020) a new argument to stopifnot, which *indeed*
is tweakable by a new option, as you can see:

stopifnot <- function(..., exprs, exprObject, local = TRUE,
                      allow.logical0 = getOption("stopifnot_allow.logical0", TRUE))
{ ## allow.logical0=TRUE: compatible w/ R <= 4.6.x; to become FALSE; at first in '--as-cran' !

    ..............................
    ..............................
    <.... some 'allow.logical0' hack in the branch for
    stopifnot(exprs = { ......
    } )
    ....>
    ..............................
    ..............................

    allTRUE <- if(allow.logical0)
		   function(x)              is.logical(x) && !anyNA(x) && all(x)
	       else
		   function(x) length(x) && is.logical(x) && !anyNA(x) && all(x)

    ... and then

    for (i in seq_len(n)) {
	r <- ...elt(i)
	if(!allTRUE(r)) {
           ............ 
           ............ 
	   stop(..............)
	   .........
       }
    }
    invisible()
} # end { stopifnot() definition }

Once I've started using this  in my "hacked" version of R-devel,
*and* set the

   options(stopifnot_allow.logical0 = FALSE)

I did need to add manually   `allow.logical0 = TRUE`
to *some* stopifnot() calls in my R code (in my packages and scripts)
and to R-core's code in base R {i.e., in the above "hacked"
branch of R-devel}.

I vaguely remember (but am not sure, not remembering details)
that the updated stopifnot() -- without setting the new option
still had some rare hickups, but I really don't remember and
also somewhat doubt my vague memory...

Maybe I should open an R bugzilla "wishlist" for this,
with my full current patch for such an enhanced stopifnot().

In any case, your issue would be solved either by explicitly adding
  allow.logical0 = FALSE
to your stopifnot() calls involving  ` <datafr>$<comp> `
or by setting the above options(stopif... = FALSE)

What do others think - about such an option for stopifnot()?

With a repeated thank you for raising the issue,
Martin


--
Martin Mächler
R Core team and ETH Zurich

Thanks Martin!

I definitely think the option for stopifnot() would help with the the first example I gave.

But the problem runs deeper than just stopifnot(). In the second example, the problem is that sum(dat$coluumn1) is 0. So stopifnot() is receiving a perfectly legitimate test that 0 < 2. and y have the same lengths and all their corresponding elements

    ..............................
    ..............................

        if(!allTRUE(r)) {
           ............
           ............
           stop(..............)
           .........
       }
    }

branch of R-devel}.

that the updated stopifnot() -- without setting the new option
still had some rare hickups, but I really don't remember and
also somewhat doubt my vague memory...

Dear all,

I agree that with Kirsten that adding the options(warnNonexistDollar=TRUE)
would be useful to catch problems outside stopifnot().

However, is it not much better to use indexing through `[`, which throws an
error for nonexistent columns?
That solves the problem of silently glossing over wrongly-spelled names and
the problem of partial matching (which it does not use).

```
dat <- data.frame(column1=1:3,column2=NA)
stopifnot(!any(is.na(dat[, "coluumn2"])))
# Error in `[.data.frame`(dat, , "coluumn2") : undefined columns selected
stopifnot(sum(dat[, "coluumn1"]) < 2)
# Error in `[.data.frame`(dat, , "coluumn1") : undefined columns selected
```

Throwing an error of course makes this approach unsuitable to check if a
column is present while simultaneously performing the assignment in the way
Martin's example did.
But first checking the presence of the name would work fine, even though it
is a bit slower:

```
if(comp %in% names(mylist)) {
    .....
    <work with> mylist["comp"]
    .....
} else {
    ## work without `mylist["comp"]  `, in some cases just
    stop("component `comp` does not exist -- cannot do xyz")
}
```

Kind regards,
Jesse

Hi Toby,

and good idea!

the attached patch (against R-devel r90842) adds predict(..., cache = TRUE)

on the span = 0.5 error, well, span was passed to predict(), which ignores it, so the fit still used 0.75. It needs to go to loess().

also, with or without the patch, the existing workspace limit stops se = TRUE at about N = 46,300 for span = 0.5 (37,800 for 0.75), so N has to stay below that

ares <- atime::atime(
  N = unique(as.integer(10^seq(1, log10(45000), by = 0.1))),
  setup = {
    set.seed(20261105)
    x <- runif(N, -3, 3)
    y <- sin(x) + rnorm(N, sd = 0.35)
    f <- loess(y ~ x, span = 0.5)
    nd <- data.frame(x = seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = 80L))
  },
  seconds.limit = 1,
  cache.FALSE = predict(f, nd, se = TRUE, cache = FALSE),
  cache.TRUE = predict(f, nd, se = TRUE, cache = TRUE))

Hi Don thanks for the update.

I tried your patch and on my machine it is definitely faster, see
figures https://github.com/tdhock/atime/issues/135#issuecomment-6748730446

It is faster for all N so as long as the increased memory usage is
acceptable, I would argue that somebody in R-core should accept the
patch.

You wrote "what still grows with N^2 is the workspace, and that is
what limits N" but the emprical memory in the figure seems to be
linear? I guess the quadratic workspace memory is using fortran not R
memory allocation? Two ideas,

1. can you please modify the code so that quadratic workspace memory
uses R memory allocation, so we can see quadratic memory usage in the
atime figure?

2. Is there a way of reducing that workspace memory from quadratic to linear?

Toby
